title: Urban heat differences enter the scientific record
what: An EPA historical review traces documented city-country temperature differences to an 1833 publication. The original publication was not opened for this review.
why: Urban form was already recognised as a source of local heat before modern climate assessments.

title: IPCC is established
what: WMO and UNEP established the IPCC to assess climate science, impacts and response options.
why: Heat would gain an enduring route into intergovernmental scientific assessment.

title: First IPCC assessment is completed
what: The first IPCC assessment was completed in August 1990. Its heat-health passages could not be reopened in this review.
why: This established the assessment cycle through which subsequent heat evidence reached governments.

title: Climate convention includes human health
what: The UNFCCC defined adverse climate effects to include harm to human health and welfare. Article 4 also addressed public health in climate response assessment.
why: Health had a treaty-level connection to climate change before heat had a dedicated global policy agenda.

title: IPCC updates its first assessment
what: The 1992 impacts supplement linked urban heat islands with global warming and discussed increased mortality from heat stress.
why: An early assessment explicitly connected city heat exposure with climate-related health risk.

title: Heat deaths expose surveillance and response gaps
what: CDC reported 465 deaths certified as heat-related during July 11-27. It also described inconsistent death definitions and the limits of medical-examiner surveillance.
why: A major urban heat emergency made preventable deaths and social vulnerability visible.

title: IPCC names direct heat-health impacts
what: The Second Assessment Report linked anticipated increases in heatwave intensity and duration to additional illness and mortality. Its Working Group II summary included a dedicated human-health section.
why: Heat-related illness and death became explicit findings in the assessment's policy summary.

title: IPCC links heatwaves with unequal impacts
what: TAR's Working Group II summary connected projected heat extremes with mortality, crop damage, cooling demand and energy reliability. Its Human Health chapter reviewed thermal stress and adaptation.
why: Heat appeared as a connected health, infrastructure and equity risk.

title: European heatwave becomes a public-health reference point
what: The 2003 European heatwave caused severe health impacts and overwhelmed hospitals in France, as reviewed by WHO and WMO. Later guidance used this event to explain heat-health warning and response needs.
why: A large mortality emergency helped turn heat prevention into a structured public-health field.

title: Fourth assessment consolidates the evidence cycle
what: The IPCC published its Fourth Assessment Report, including a Synthesis Report. Detailed heat passages were inaccessible in this review and are listed as verification gaps.
why: Heat's assessment history continued within a regular science-policy cycle, although this entry makes no new heat-confidence claim.

title: WHO publishes heat-health action-plan guidance
what: WHO's EuroHEAT guidance brought warnings, public advice, health services, housing and urban planning into one prevention framework.
why: Protection became a planned portfolio of public actions rather than a weather advisory alone.

title: Russian heatwave reinforces the public-health case
what: The 2010 Russian heatwave became another major example in WHO-WMO guidance on severe heat-health impacts.
why: Repeated emergencies strengthened the case for warning systems linked to health action.

title: Ahmedabad heatwave prompts coordinated planning
what: Following a deadly May heatwave, Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation and partners began developing a coordinated response.
why: A South Asian city linked a local health emergency to municipal heat governance.

title: Theory identifies a limit to heat adaptation
what: A peer-reviewed study proposed sustained 35°C wet-bulb exposure as a theoretical limit under idealised conditions. This was not a general safety threshold for everyday activity.
why: Humid heat introduced physical limits to adaptation into climate-risk discussions.

title: SREX policy summary is approved
what: IPCC member governments approved the SREX Summary for Policymakers in Kampala. The announcement connected disaster risk management, adaptation and vulnerability.
why: Extreme events gained an assessment organised around risk and the capacity to cope.

title: SREX becomes a published assessment
what: The published SREX brought climate extremes, exposure, vulnerability and disaster management into a shared assessment.
why: It provided a bridge between physical hazard science and disaster-risk practice.

title: AR5 physical-science assessment is published
what: AR5 Working Group I assessed human contributions to temperature extremes and increasing heatwave frequency in large parts of Europe, Asia and Australia.
why: Observed heat trends and attribution became increasingly central to the assessment story.

title: Ahmedabad launches its heat action plan
what: The municipal corporation and partners launched a plan with health-department coordination, forecasting, alerts and public communication. WHO-WMO describe it as South Asia's first comprehensive city heat-health plan; that bounded claim is retained as claimed.
why: South Asian municipal experience became a reference for organised heat protection.

title: AR5 connects heat with work capacity
what: The AR5 assessment linked heat-related health risks with lost work capacity and reduced labour productivity in vulnerable populations.
why: Heat became more visible as a livelihood and economic risk alongside mortality.

title: AR5 synthesis strengthens the heat signal
what: AR5 judged increased heatwave frequency likely in large parts of Europe, Asia and Australia. It judged future increases in heatwave frequency and duration very likely.
why: Heat appeared as both an observed change and a continuing future risk.

title: Paris Agreement establishes the adaptation goal
what: Article 7 established the global goal on adaptation, covering capacity, resilience and vulnerability. The opened UNFCCC workstream record confirms this institutional milestone.
why: Heat adaptation gained a wider international policy framework without becoming a separate treaty obligation.

title: Severe Indian heat reinforces national planning needs
what: A severe heatwave affected India during the 2015 hot season. WMO's retrospective account linked the regional emergency with subsequent heat-health planning.
why: South Asian heat deaths became a visible reason to connect forecasts, health agencies and disaster management.

title: WHO and WMO integrate warnings with health action
what: Joint guidance covered heat-health warning-system development, epidemiology, biometeorology and risk communication. The PDF is dated 2015, while WHO's landing page is dated 2016.
why: Weather and health services gained a shared technical basis for heat warnings.

title: Disaster framework centres lives, livelihoods and health
what: The Sendai Framework adopted targets for reducing disaster risk and losses in lives, livelihoods and health. It is an all-hazards framework, rather than a heat-specific agreement.
why: Heat protection could be connected to broader disaster governance and loss monitoring.

title: Karachi emergency exposes coordination needs
what: The June heatwave exposed gaps in inter-agency coordination and clarity of response roles. A later management plan drew on analysis of this event.
why: Heat entered city disaster planning through an identified institutional gap.

title: South Asian experts convene on heat and health
what: A South Asian workshop in Colombo discussed heat-health practice and the need for an integrated approach. The later GHHIN forum record identifies it as a precursor meeting.
why: South Asian practice contributed to the formation of a global heat-health exchange.

title: Global heat-health network is founded
what: WMO, WHO, NOAA and partners founded GHHIN. Its current history distinguishes founding in 2016 from later public launch and forum milestones.
why: Heat acquired a dedicated international community linking science, services and policy.

title: India circulates national heat-action planning guidance
what: NDMA circulated guidance to state disaster-management agencies for preparing, implementing and evaluating heat action plans.
why: City experience entered a national framework for seasonal heat protection.

title: Disaster-loss inventory gains Sendai alignment
what: UNDRR upgraded DesInventar to DesInventar Sendai, supporting subnational disaster-loss recording.
why: Local loss records offered a complement to international databases that depend on event visibility and reporting thresholds.

title: Karachi heatwave management plan is delivered
what: ESSA and The Urban Unit delivered the city's management plan between November 2016 and April 2017, with CDKN support. GHHIN records city approval and a proposed evaluation framework.
why: The response moved from emergency experience to defined responsibilities before, during and after heat.

place: South Asia, including the Indus and Ganges basins
title: Humid-heat projections focus on South Asian agriculture
what: A modelling study projected dangerous wet-bulb extremes in densely populated agricultural regions under high future emissions. It connected hazard with poverty and exposure.
why: South Asia entered a prominent scientific debate about humid heat and human adaptation limits.

title: Annual indicators make heat losses trackable
what: The Lancet Countdown reported heat exposure and labour-capacity indicators within a 41-indicator framework. Its 2018 report gave a heat-related labour-loss estimate for 2017.
why: Recurring indicators made heat a continuing health-development issue beyond individual emergencies.

title: Half a degree becomes a protection question
what: UNFCCC's response to SR1.5 highlighted substantially lower severe-heatwave exposure at 1.5°C than at 2°C. The original report's detailed heat passages remained inaccessible.
why: Temperature goals became easier to connect with differences in human heat exposure.

title: GHHIN holds its inaugural global forum
what: The forum ran from 17 to 20 December, with a Southeast Asian regional focus and attention to communication. Its description distinguishes the formal launch from earlier founding.
why: Regional experience entered a shared global heat-health agenda.

title: ILO quantifies future heat-related working-hour losses
what: ILO projected that 2.2 per cent of global working hours would be lost in 2030 under its stated assumptions. Southern Asia was among the regions with the largest projected losses.
why: Heat became legible to labour, development and economic policy through a common work metric.

title: Land report connects heat with food systems
what: SRCCL assessed increased frequency, intensity and duration of heat-related events in most land regions with high confidence. It linked climate pressures with land degradation and food security.
why: Heat was embedded in land and food-system risk rather than treated only as a health emergency.

title: Ocean assessment expands the meaning of heat risk
what: AFD's official review records adoption of SROCC and its policy summary on this date. It describes assessment of ocean and cryosphere impacts, human societies and adaptation; original heat-specific wording was not reopened.
why: The history of heat risk widened to ocean-linked ecosystems and coastal livelihoods.

title: Observations reveal exceptional humid-heat episodes
what: A station-based study found brief, local humid-heat extremes near or above the theoretical 35°C wet-bulb benchmark. These were not evidence of sustained exposure across whole regions.
why: A risk often discussed as distant future became an observed, locally concentrated phenomenon.

title: AR6 raises confidence in observed hot extremes
what: Working Group I judged increased frequency and intensity of hot extremes across most land since the 1950s virtually certain. It assessed human-induced climate change as the main driver with high confidence.
why: The global heat signal and its human cause became much more firmly established.

title: Study attributes part of heat mortality to warming
what: A study of 732 locations in 43 countries estimated that 37.0% of warm-season heat-related deaths in its study countries were attributable to human-induced climate change during 1991-2018.
why: Climate attribution extended from weather hazards to observed health burdens.

title: Northwestern heatwave demonstrates rapid health surveillance
what: CDC recorded 2,779 heat-related emergency-department visits during June 25-30 in its northwestern surveillance region. It highlighted near-real-time surveillance for guiding response.
why: A rare regional event showed how heat can rapidly exceed familiar health-service expectations.

title: Bibliometrics documents rapidly growing heatwave research
what: A review analysed 8,011 Web of Science papers and reported that the research literature doubled within about 5 years. It noted prominent attention to events in 1995 and 2003.
why: Scientific attention became measurable, although publication growth does not establish growth in public or media attention.

title: Experiments challenge the 35°C wet-bulb shorthand
what: A study first published online in December 2021, with a February 2022 issue date, found uncompensable heat stress below 35°C wet-bulb in young healthy adults doing light activity. The experiments did not establish one universal safety limit.
why: Physiological evidence narrowed the gap between a theoretical survivability limit and real exposure risk.

title: AR6 connects heat with vulnerability and livelihoods
what: Working Group II assessed health, cities, livelihoods and Asia in dedicated chapters. The opened UNFCCC summary also presented exposure to hyperthermia from extreme heat and humidity.
why: Heat risk became more clearly connected to vulnerability, settlement conditions and adaptation limits.

title: Mitigation assessment recognises urban heat trade-offs
what: Working Group III assessed urban planning options that can reduce heat-island effects. It also noted that increased density can increase heatwave vulnerability, with high confidence.
why: Climate responses themselves became part of the heat-risk discussion.

title: WMO carries rapid South Asian heat attribution
what: WMO communicated a rapid study finding that the 2022 regional heat event was about 30 times more likely because of climate change. It also described linked health, agriculture and water impacts.
why: South Asian heat entered an international attribution conversation during the event's immediate aftermath.

title: Global Cooling Pledge is launched
what: The COP28 Presidency and UNEP Cool Coalition launched the Global Cooling Pledge. UNEP later described its combined cooling-emissions and access aims.
why: Protection from heat and the climate impacts of cooling entered a shared international initiative.

title: Income-protection insurance for women is announced
what: SEWA, Arsht-Rock and Blue Marble announced parametric extreme-heat income insurance. The announcement included premium support and design funding; it was not proof of payouts or long-term viability.
why: Heat protection explicitly connected women's health with the income lost when work becomes unsafe.

title: AR6 synthesis brings risk and equity together
what: The Synthesis integrated the three working groups and three special reports. UNCCD's opened record highlighted disproportionate climate impacts on vulnerable communities.
why: Heat entered a synthesis connecting physical risk, development conditions and unequal impacts.

title: Heat-insurance pilot moves into coverage
what: Arsht-Rock's project record dates the launch with SEWA and Blue Marble to May 2023 and reports first-year coverage for 21,000 members.
why: An announced financial instrument became an implemented pilot, with outcomes still distinct from coverage.

title: Dhaka North announces a chief heat officer
what: Arsht-Rock and Dhaka North announced a dedicated chief heat officer role to coordinate heat responses. The partner announcement describes it as the first in Asia; independent confirmation of that regional first was not established.
why: Heat gained a named coordination function in a major South Asian city.

title: Singapore introduces heat-stress measures for outdoor work
what: Measures took immediate effect and included hourly WBGT monitoring. Heavy physical work at WBGT of 32°C or higher required at least 10 minutes of hourly rest under shade.
why: Heat protection became an explicit employer responsibility with an operational exposure trigger.

title: Adaptation framework includes health and social protection
what: Decision 2/CMA.5 set targets covering health resilience, climate-related morbidity and mortality, and adaptive social protection. It did not establish a separate heat-finance entitlement.
why: Negotiated adaptation goals created policy space for health and livelihood protection from heat.

title: COP28 holds its inaugural Health Day
what: WHO recorded the inaugural Health Day and the COP28 climate-and-health declaration. The declaration is separate from negotiated COP decisions.
why: Health gained a dedicated and highly visible place in the COP programme.

title: Nepal specifies responsibilities for heat response
what: NDRRMA's plan assigned actions for warnings, local health teams, schools, power, workplaces and daily-wage workers. The opened English copy carries a 2024 plan year; its upload path is later.
why: Heat entered a multisector national response matrix in a Himalayan country.

title: Bangladesh launches national heat-illness guidance
what: DGHS, supported by UNICEF, launched national guidance with attention to children and pregnant women.
why: Heat response became more explicitly connected to primary care and maternal and child health.

title: ILO highlights chronic workplace heat exposure
what: ILO's Heat at work report reviewed science, policy and legislation in 21 countries. It reported that eight in ten occupational injuries from extreme heat happened outside heatwaves.
why: Routine hot work became visible alongside exceptional heatwave emergencies.

title: UN call places extreme heat across sectors
what: The UN Secretary-General's call addressed vulnerable people, workers, resilience through data and science, and limiting warming. WHO's account linked it with preventable heat illness and mortality.
why: Extreme heat became a named UN-wide action issue spanning health, work and climate.

title: Adaptation indicators become a shared monitoring framework
what: UNFCCC records adoption of 59 Belém Adaptation Indicators at CMA7. These cover adaptation more broadly and are not 59 heat indicators.
why: Adaptation visibility increasingly depended on measurable progress as well as declarations.

title: Southeast Asia heat-health hub gains public launch
what: Singapore's official account records the inaugural regional forum and the NUS-hosted GHHIN Southeast Asia Hub. This entry dates the public launch, rather than the earliest preparatory work.
why: Humid tropical heat gained a dedicated regional science-policy home.

title: UNEP and Brazil launch city heat initiative
what: UNEP and the COP30 Presidency launched Beat the Heat in Cities. Italy also pledged EUR 2 million for Global Cooling Pledge support.
why: Heat action gained an international implementation initiative connecting cities and sustainable cooling.

title: WHO-WMO issue workplace heat guidance
what: The agencies released technical guidance on climate change and workplace heat stress. It connected prevention with worker health, safety and locally relevant action.
why: Heat-health practice broadened beyond city alerts into the organisation of work.

title: World Bank launches heat-health and economy assessment
what: The report drew on climate data and a two-round 2024 household survey of more than 16,000 people. It estimated 250 million workdays lost and economic losses up to $1.78 billion in 2024.
why: Heat became a quantified national development and human-capital issue.

title: Belém health plan centres equity and implementation
what: WHO records the launch of the Belém Health Action Plan at COP30 Health Day. Its stated foundations included equity, climate justice and participatory governance.
why: The climate-health agenda moved further into adaptation delivery and the distribution of protection.

title: Heat resilience gains a dedicated financing framework
what: UNDRR and NDMA India, with technical support from the Centre for Disaster Protection, published Financing heat resilience. It covered public budgets, concessional finance, private capital and risk-transfer instruments.
why: The question expanded from which heat actions exist to how different protection functions are financed.

title: Disaster review makes heat-reporting delays explicit
what: CRED's 2025 disaster review, with a 17 March 2026 reference date, recorded zero extreme-temperature deaths in its provisional table. It explicitly said reporting delays had left many heatwave deaths uncounted.
why: A zero in a disaster table became a documented data gap, rather than evidence of no heat deaths.

title: WHO updates the heat-health planning framework
what: WHO reports a second edition of its heat-health action-plan guidance, organised around eight core elements. Governance, financing, surveillance and review are explicit components.
why: A plan was framed more clearly as an operating system for sustained protection.

title: South Asia heat-health hub is launched
what: GHHIN and CEEW announced a Wellcome-funded regional hub with coordinating partners spanning research, policy and public health.
why: South Asian evidence and local practice gained a dedicated route into regional and global exchange.

title: Cities special-report draft enters expert review
what: The European Commission's official account records review of the Cities Special Report's second-order draft from 8 May to 3 July. It gave March 2027 as the planned final release date.
why: Cities were receiving a dedicated assessment process, but draft material was not an approved finding.

title: WMO frames heat within Asian multi-hazard risk
what: WMO released its State of the Climate in Asia 2025 account, connecting dangerous heat, ocean warming, glaciers and early warnings.
why: Heat was embedded in a regional account of interacting risks to health, food, infrastructure and livelihoods.

title: Heat monitoring expands to mothers and children
what: WHO, WMO, UNICEF and UNFPA published priority indicators for monitoring heat impacts on maternal, newborn and child health. The framework links health data with heat-exposure measures.
why: Previously less visible outcomes gained a dedicated monitoring approach.
